analysis.one_liner: Funds federal gun violence research and lost-gun tracking with a $1 background-check fee.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing or a vote; it sat in House committees until the Congress ended with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have added a $1 fee to each federal background check for a gun purchase. The money from those fees — the first $10 million a year — would go to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention to study gun violence, with the next $5 million covering the cost of running the background check system itself and the rest going to the FBI's victim assistance office. It would also require gun owners to tell local police within 48 hours if a firearm is lost or stolen, with police entering the report into the FBI's national crime database, and it would impose fines or jail time for failing to report. The bill was referred to House committees and never advanced.
analysis.who_benefits: Communities affected by gun violence gain better federal research into its causes, funded without new appropriations. Victims of gun violence gain funding for the FBI's victim assistance office. Police gain faster reporting of stolen guns, which helps trace crime guns. Gun buyers pay only $1 per background check transaction.

how_it_helps.text: It would fund CDC gun violence research through the fee revenue, with the first $10 million a year going to the CDC without needing a separate appropriation.
It would require gun owners to report lost or stolen firearms within 48 hours, with reports forwarded to the FBI's national crime database, making it easier to trace guns used in crimes.
Remaining fee revenue after research and background-check system costs would go to the FBI's Office for Victim Assistance.

analysis.who_pays: Gun buyers pay a $1 fee per background-check transaction. Licensed dealers bear a paperwork duty to collect, receipt, and remit the fee, with $2,500 civil penalties for failures. Gun owners who lose a firearm and do not report it within 48 hours face a fine of up to $10,000 or up to a year in prison per gun.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun buyers, dealers, and gun owners

drawbacks.text: The bill adds a $1 fee to every background check for gun buyers and creates a $2,500 civil penalty for dealers who fail to collect it, a small new cost on firearm purchases.
Gun owners who do not report a lost or stolen gun within 48 hours of discovery would face a fine of up to $10,000 or up to a year in prison per firearm, a new criminal liability for an oversight.
The lost/stolen reporting requirement applies to ordinary gun owners, not just dealers, with penalties per firearm.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The costs to the public are small and spread out (a one-dollar-per-transaction fee, a duty to report a lost gun) while the benefits — better data on gun violence, faster tracing of lost and stolen guns, funding for victims — fall on everyone. The bill was modest by gun-policy standards, and it did not fund victim assistance directly but routed funds to an FBI office. The real weakness is not design but fate: it was so narrowly backed that it never got a hearing, let alone a vote.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to two House committees and their subcommittees, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Nydia Velazquez introduced the bill on February 2, 2022, and it was referred to the House Judiciary and Energy and Commerce Committees.
No other House member signed on as a cosponsor.
The bill's only further actions were referrals to the Health subcommittee and, in November 2022, the Crime subcommittee of Judiciary; neither advanced it.
The 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill expired without floor action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The gun industry faces no new background-check fee or lost-and-stolen reporting mandate, and gun owners face no new reporting requirement or penalties. Gun violence research and victim-assistance funding that the bill would have raised went unfunded.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Gun industry and gun owners; nothing changed

sides.party_line_note: With a single sponsor and no cosponsors, no recorded vote, and no recorded opposition, the bill's partisan shape cannot be measured from the record.

industries.note: Dealers would collect and remit a $1 background-check fee with a $2,500 penalty for failing to do so, and would face a national reporting net for lost and stolen guns. The fee is small but the compliance and penalty provisions add regulation to the industry.

Owners would owe a new $1 fee per transaction and would face fines or jail time for failing to report a lost or stolen gun within 48 hours. This is a modest cost paired with a public-safety requirement.
